claim: Cell division and basement membrane invasion are mutually exclusive cellular behaviors.
source: A growing body of evidence suggests that cell division and basement membrane invasion are mutually exclusive cellular behaviors.
evidence: The manuscript cites this as a growing body of evidence from the literature.

claim: The anchor cell is post-mitotic and invasive.
source: the post-mitotic, invasive anchor cell
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by established knowledge of C. elegans development.

claim: Ventral uterine (VU) cells are proliferative and non-invasive.
source: the neighboring proliferative, non-invasive ventral uterine (VU) cells
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by established knowledge of C. elegans development.

claim: NHR-67 levels are important for discriminating between invasive and proliferative behavior.
source: levels of NHR-67 are important for discriminating between invasive and proliferative behavior
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Transcription of NHR-67 is downregulated following post-translational degradation of HLH-2 in VU cells.
source: Transcription of NHR-67 is downregulated following post-translational degradation of its direct upstream regulator, HLH-2 (E/Daughterless) in VU cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Residual NHR-67 protein in VU cells is compartmentalized into discrete punctae that are dynamic over the cell cycle.
source: In the nuclei of VU cells, residual NHR-67 protein is compartmentalized into discrete punctae that are dynamic over the cell cycle
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by imaging data in Figure 3.

claim: NHR-67 punctae exhibit liquid-like properties.
source: residual NHR-67 protein is compartmentalized into discrete punctae that are dynamic over the cell cycle and exhibit liquid-like properties
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by FRAP and time-lapse imaging data in Figure 3.

claim: UNC-37 and LSY-22 are homologs of the transcriptional co-repressor Groucho.
source: homologs of the transcriptional co-repressor Groucho (UNC-37 and LSY-22)
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is based on established knowledge of protein homology.

claim: POP-1 is the TCF/LEF homolog in C. elegans.
source: the TCF/LEF homolog POP-1
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is based on established knowledge of protein homology.

claim: UNC-37, LSY-22, and POP-1 colocalize with NHR-67 punctae.
source: By screening for proteins that colocalize with NHR-67 punctae, we identified new regulators of uterine cell fate maintenance: homologs of the transcriptional co-repressor Groucho (UNC-37 and LSY-22), as well as the TCF/LEF homolog POP-1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by colocalization data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The association of NHR-67 with the Groucho/TCF complex suppresses the default invasive state in non-invasive cells.
source: We propose a model in which the association of NHR-67 with the Groucho/TCF complex suppresses the default invasive state in non-invasive cells
evidence: This is a proposed model based on inference from the experimental data presented.

claim: Switching between invasive and proliferative phenotypes has been observed in melanoma.
source: Switching between invasive and proliferative phenotypes has been observed in melanoma and recently in breast cancer (Hoek et al., 2008; Mondal et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Switching between invasive and proliferative phenotypes has been observed in breast cancer.
source: Switching between invasive and proliferative phenotypes has been observed in melanoma and recently in breast cancer (Hoek et al., 2008; Mondal et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Z1.pp and Z4.aa give rise to four cells that will adopt one of two cellular fates: a proliferative VU cell or the terminally differentiated, invasive anchor cell (AC).
source: the proximal granddaughters of the Z1 and Z4 somatic gonad progenitors, Z1.pp and Z4.aa, give rise to four cells that will adopt one of two cellular fates: a proliferative VU cell or the terminally differentiated, invasive anchor cell (AC) (Figure 1A; Kimble and Hirsh, 1979)
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 1A and supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Z1.ppa and Z4.aap quickly lose their bipotentiality and become VU cells.
source: The distal cells of this competency group, Z1.ppa and Z4.aap, quickly lose their bipotentiality and become VU cells (Seydoux et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Z1.ppp and Z4.aaa undergo a stochastic Notch-mediated cell fate decision, giving rise to another VU cell and the post-mitotic AC.
source: the proximal cells, Z1.ppp and Z4.aaa, undergo a stochastic Notch-mediated cell fate decision, giving rise to another VU cell and the post-mitotic AC (Figure 1A and B; Greenwald et al., 1983; Seydoux and Greenwald, 1989)
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 1A and B and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The AC breaches the underlying basement membrane, connecting the uterus to the vulval epithelium to facilitate egg-laying.
source: Following fate specification, the AC undergoes invasive differentiation and breaches the underlying basement membrane, connecting the uterus to the vulval epithelium to facilitate egg-laying (Figure 1B; Sherwood and Sternberg, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 1B and supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The AC is the default cell fate of the somatic gonad.
source: The AC is the default cell fate of the somatic gonad, as disruption of Notch or Wnt signaling results in ectopic AC specification (Phillips et al., 2007; Seydoux and Greenwald, 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Disruption of Notch or Wnt signaling results in ectopic AC specification.
source: The AC is the default cell fate of the somatic gonad, as disruption of Notch or Wnt signaling results in ectopic AC specification (Phillips et al., 2007; Seydoux and Greenwald, 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: AC invasion is dependent on G0 cell cycle arrest.
source: Our previous work has shown that AC invasion is dependent on G0 cell cycle arrest, which is coordinated by the pro-invasive transcription factor NHR-67 (NR2E1/TLX) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Matus et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to a figure supplement and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: NHR-67 coordinates G0 cell cycle arrest in the AC.
source: Our previous work has shown that AC invasion is dependent on G0 cell cycle arrest, which is coordinated by the pro-invasive transcription factor NHR-67 (NR2E1/TLX) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Matus et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to a figure supplement and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: NHR-67 functions within a gene regulatory network comprised of four conserved transcription factors.
source: NHR-67 functions within a gene regulatory network comprised of four conserved transcription factors whose homologs have been implicated in several types of metastatic cancer (Liang and Wang, 2020; Milde-Langosch, 2005; Nelson et al., 2021; Wang and Baker, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Homologs of the transcription factors in the NHR-67 gene regulatory network have been implicated in several types of metastatic cancer.
source: NHR-67 functions within a gene regulatory network comprised of four conserved transcription factors whose homologs have been implicated in several types of metastatic cancer (Liang and Wang, 2020; Milde-Langosch, 2005; Nelson et al., 2021; Wang and Baker, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: NHR-67 is regulated by a feed-forward loop formed by EGL-43 and HLH-2.
source: We previously reported that NHR-67 is regulated by a feed-forward loop formed by EGL-43 (Evi1) and HLH-2 (E/Daughterless), which functions largely in parallel to a cell cycle-independent subcircuit controlled by FOS-1 (Fos) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Medwig-Kinney et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to a figure supplement and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The EGL-43/HLH-2 feed-forward loop functions largely in parallel to a cell cycle-independent subcircuit controlled by FOS-1.
source: We previously reported that NHR-67 is regulated by a feed-forward loop formed by EGL-43 (Evi1) and HLH-2 (E/Daughterless), which functions largely in parallel to a cell cycle-independent subcircuit controlled by FOS-1 (Fos) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Medwig-Kinney et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to a figure supplement and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: EGL-43, HLH-2, and NHR-67 function to independently regulate LIN-12 (Notch) signaling during the initial AC/VU cell fate decision.
source: EGL-43, HLH-2, and NHR-67 are reiteratively used within the Z lineage of the somatic gonad, in that, they also function to independently regulate LIN-12 (Notch) signaling during the initial AC/VU cell fate decision (Medwig-Kinney et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Expression of LIN-12 is not absolutely required for VU cell fate.
source: Despite its role in lateral inhibition between Z1.ppp and Z4.aaa, expression of LIN-12 is not absolutely required for VU cell fate (Sallee et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Arresting VU cells in G0 through ectopic expression of CKI-1 does not make them invasive.
source: Cell cycle state also cannot explain the difference between AC and VU cell fates, as arresting VU cells in G0 through ectopic expression of CKI-1 (p21/p27) does not make them invasive (Smith et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: VU cells express approximately 89% of AC expression levels of EGL-43.
source: EGL-43 was also not a promising candidate, as it is expressed in both cell types at comparable levels, with VU cells exhibiting approximately 89% of AC expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to figure supplement data.

claim: VU cells express merely 17% of HLH-2 levels observed in the AC.
source: In contrast, HLH-2 exhibits significant asymmetry in expression, as VU cells express merely 17% of HLH-2 levels observed in the AC (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 1C and D.

claim: Dimerization-driven degradation of HLH-2 is responsible for its downregulation in the VU cells.
source: Previous studies have shown that dimerization-driven degradation of HLH-2 is responsible for its downregulation in the VU cells (Benavidez et al., 2022; Karp and Greenwald, 2003; Sallee and Greenwald, 2015b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: NHR-67 exhibits over threefold enrichment in the AC compared to VU cells.
source: NHR-67 exhibits a similar pattern of expression with over threefold enrichment in the AC, consistent with prior observations of transgenic reporters (Figure 1C and D; Verghese et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 1C and D and supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Strong depletion of NHR-67 through RNAi treatment results in ACs adopting VU-like characteristics.
source: We found that strong depletion of NHR-67 through RNA interference (RNAi) treatment results in ACs adopting VU-like characteristics.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by experimental data in Figure 1E.

claim: LIN-12 (Notch) normally becomes restricted to the VU cells during AC/VU cell fate specification.
source: During AC/VU cell fate specification, LIN-12 (Notch) normally becomes restricted to the VU cells while the Delta-like ligand LAG-2 (visualized by LAG-2::P2A::H2B::mTurquoise2 Medwig-Kinney et al., 2022) accumulates in the AC (Wilkinson et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The Delta-like ligand LAG-2 accumulates in the AC during AC/VU cell fate specification.
source: During AC/VU cell fate specification, LIN-12 (Notch) normally becomes restricted to the VU cells while the Delta-like ligand LAG-2 (visualized by LAG-2::P2A::H2B::mTurquoise2 Medwig-Kinney et al., 2022) accumulates in the AC (Wilkinson et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: NHR-67 deficient ACs ectopically expressed membrane-localized Notch.
source: Here, we observe that NHR-67 deficient ACs not only proliferated and failed to invade, as reported previously (Matus et al., 2015), but also ectopically expressed membrane-localized Notch (visualized by LIN-12::mNeonGreen Pani et al., 2022; Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to figures and supported by citations.

claim: NHR-67-deficient ACs expressed both LIN-12 and LAG-2, potentially indicating an intermediate state between AC and VU cell fate.
source: Notably, NHR-67-deficient ACs expressed both LIN-12 and LAG-2, potentially indicating an intermediate state between AC and VU cell fate (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to figures and represents an interpretation of the data.

claim: Ectopic expression of NHR-67 ubiquitously following AC/VU specification resulted in the presence of multiple invasive ACs at approximately 5% penetrance.
source: Next, we ectopically expressed NHR-67 ubiquitously following AC/VU specification using a heat shock inducible transgene (hsp::NHR-67::2x-BFP) (Medwig-Kinney et al., 2020) and observed the presence of multiple invasive ACs at a low penetrance (approximately 5%, n>50), denoted by ectopic expression of an AC marker (cdh-3p::mCherry::moeABD) and expansion of the basement membrane gap (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 1F and supported by experimental data.

claim: Proliferative ACs cannot invade.
source: As previous work has demonstrated that proliferative ACs cannot invade (Matus et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Invasive ectopic ACs arising from NHR-67 overexpression most likely arose from the fate conversion of neighboring VU cells.
source: As previous work has demonstrated that proliferative ACs cannot invade (Matus et al., 2015), we concluded that these invasive ectopic ACs most likely arose from the fate conversion of neighboring VU cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and prior knowledge.

claim: HLH-2 positively regulates NHR-67 expression in the context of the AC.
source: We and others have previously shown that HLH-2 positively regulates NHR-67 expression in the context of the AC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Bodofsky et al., 2018; Medwig-Kinney et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to a figure supplement and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The initial onset of HLH-2 is asymmetric in Z1.pp and Z4.aa.
source: In support of this hypothesis, we found that the initial onset of HLH-2, which has been shown to be asymmetric in Z1.pp and Z4.aa (Attner et al., 2019), correlates to onset of an NHR-67 transgene (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Gerstein et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to a figure supplement and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The initial onset of HLH-2 correlates to onset of an NHR-67 transgene.
source: In support of this hypothesis, we found that the initial onset of HLH-2, which has been shown to be asymmetric in Z1.pp and Z4.aa (Attner et al., 2019), correlates to onset of an NHR-67 transgene (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Gerstein et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to a figure supplement and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Ectopic expression of HLH-2 using a heat shock inducible transgene resulted in elevated NHR-67 expression in VU cells (43% increase).
source: To test whether HLH-2 degradation is responsible for NHR-67 downregulation in the VU, we drove ectopic expression of HLH-2 using a transgene under the control of a heat shock inducible promoter (hsp::HLH-2::2x-BFP) (Medwig-Kinney et al., 2020) and observed elevated NHR-67 expression in VU cells (43% increase; n>30) (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 2A and B and represents experimental data.

claim: UBA-1 is an E1 ubiquitin-activating enzyme that is necessary for HLH-2 degradation in VU cells.
source: To control against potential dimerization-driven degradation of HLH-2 in the VU cells, which the heat shock inducible transgene would still be susceptible to, we disrupted UBA-1, an E1 ubiquitin-activating enzyme that has recently been shown to be necessary for HLH-2 degradation in VU cells (Benavidez et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Following perturbation of UBA-1 through RNAi treatment, HLH-2 expression in the VU cells increased more than fourfold.
source: Following perturbation of UBA-1 through RNAi treatment, HLH-2 expression in the VU cells increased more than fourfold and NHR-67 expression increased by nearly 60% compared to the empty vector control (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to figure supplement data.

claim: Following perturbation of UBA-1 through RNAi treatment, NHR-67 expression increased by nearly 60% compared to the empty vector control.
source: Following perturbation of UBA-1 through RNAi treatment, HLH-2 expression in the VU cells increased more than fourfold and NHR-67 expression increased by nearly 60% compared to the empty vector control (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to figure supplement data.

claim: A 276 bp region of the NHR-67 promoter is required for NHR-67 expression in the uterine tissue.
source: This is based on the identification of E binding motifs within a 276 bp region of the NHR-67 promoter that is required for NHR-67 expression in the uterine tissue and encompasses the location of several hypomorphic mutations (pf2, pf88, pf159) (Figure 2C; Bodofsky et al., 2018; Verghese et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 2C and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The 276 bp region of the NHR-67 promoter encompasses the location of several hypomorphic mutations (pf2, pf88, pf159).
source: This is based on the identification of E binding motifs within a 276 bp region of the NHR-67 promoter that is required for NHR-67 expression in the uterine tissue and encompasses the location of several hypomorphic mutations (pf2, pf88, pf159) (Figure 2C; Bodofsky et al., 2018; Verghese et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 2C and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: HLH-2 is capable of binding directly to the 276 bp region of the NHR-67 promoter.
source: Yeast growth on the selective SC-HIS-TRP plates containing the competitive inhibitor 3-aminotriazole (3-AT) suggests that HLH-2 is capable of binding directly to this 276 bp region of the NHR-67 promoter (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 2D and represents experimental data from a yeast one-hybrid assay.

claim: NHR-67 localization is fairly uniform throughout the AC nucleus (excluding the nucleolus).
source: While NHR-67 localization is fairly uniform throughout the AC nucleus (excluding the nucleolus), we often observed discrete punctae throughout the nuclei of VU cells (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 3A and B and represents observational data.

claim: Discrete NHR-67 punctae are often observed throughout the nuclei of VU cells.
source: While NHR-67 localization is fairly uniform throughout the AC nucleus (excluding the nucleolus), we often observed discrete punctae throughout the nuclei of VU cells (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 3A and B and represents observational data.

claim: NHR-67 punctae were observed with NHR-67 endogenously tagged with several different fluorescent proteins, including GFP, mNeonGreen, mScarlet-I, and TagRFP-T.
source: These punctae were observed with NHR-67 endogenously tagged with several different fluorescent proteins, including GFP, mNeonGreen, mScarlet-I, and TagRFP-T (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to figure supplement data.

claim: NHR-67 punctae are not an artifact of the fluorophore or sample preparation.
source: These punctae were observed with NHR-67 endogenously tagged with several different fluorescent proteins, including GFP, mNeonGreen, mScarlet-I, and TagRFP-T (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B) and in the absence of tissue fixation methods that can cause artificial puncta (Irgen-Gioro et al., 2022), suggesting that they are not an artifact of the fluorophore or sample preparation.
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to figure supplement data and a citation, representing an inference from the data.

claim: The number of NHR-67 punctae was dynamic over the course of the cell cycle, with punctae first appearing shortly after mitotic exit in the G1 phase.
source: Time-lapse microscopy revealed that the number of NHR-67 punctae was dynamic over the course of the cell cycle, with punctae first appearing shortly after mitotic exit in the G1 phase, and then reducing in number to two large punctae prior to nuclear envelope breakdown before disappearing (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 3D and E and represents time-lapse imaging data.

claim: NHR-67 punctae reduce in number to two large punctae prior to nuclear envelope breakdown before disappearing.
source: Time-lapse microscopy revealed that the number of NHR-67 punctae was dynamic over the course of the cell cycle, with punctae first appearing shortly after mitotic exit in the G1 phase, and then reducing in number to two large punctae prior to nuclear envelope breakdown before disappearing (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 3D and E and represents time-lapse imaging data.

claim: NHR-67 punctae exhibit fusion or condensation prior to their dissolution.
source: We collected additional recordings with finer time resolution and captured fusion, or condensation, of punctae prior to their dissolution (representative of 6 biological replicates) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 3F and represents time-lapse imaging data.

claim: NHR-67 punctae exhibit relatively rapid diffusion kinetics with a half-time of fluorescence recovery of 46 seconds.
source: These punctae also exhibit relatively rapid diffusion kinetics, as observed by fluorescence recovery following photobleaching (t1/2=46 s; n=8) at a rate within the same order of magnitude as P granule proteins PGL-1 and PGL-3 (Figure 3G and H; Putnam et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 3G and H and represents FRAP experimental data.

claim: The fluorescence recovery rate of NHR-67 punctae is within the same order of magnitude as P granule proteins PGL-1 and PGL-3.
source: These punctae also exhibit relatively rapid diffusion kinetics, as observed by fluorescence recovery following photobleaching (t1/2=46 s; n=8) at a rate within the same order of magnitude as P granule proteins PGL-1 and PGL-3 (Figure 3G and H; Putnam et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 3G and H and supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: There is no significant colocalization between NHR-67 and AMA-1 punctae (Manders' overlap coefficient, M=0.066).
source: To test this hypothesis, we co-visualized NHR-67 with a GFP-tagged allele of ama-1, the amanitin-binding subunit of RNA polymerase II (Hills-Muckey et al., 2022) and failed to observe significant colocalization between NHR-67 and AMA-1 punctae (Manders' overlap coefficient, M=0.066) compared to negative controls where a single channel was compared to its 90-degree rotation (M=0.108) (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 4A and B and represents colocalization analysis data.

claim: There is no significant colocalization of NHR-67 with the endogenously tagged HP1 heterochromatin protein HPL-1 (M=0.076).
source: However, we did not observe significant colocalization of NHR-67 with the endogenously tagged HP1 heterochromatin proteins (Patel and Hobert, 2017) HPL-1 (M=0.076) or HPL-2 (M=0.083) (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 4A and B and represents colocalization analysis data.

claim: There is no significant colocalization of NHR-67 with the endogenously tagged HP1 heterochromatin protein HPL-2 (M=0.083).
source: However, we did not observe significant colocalization of NHR-67 with the endogenously tagged HP1 heterochromatin proteins (Patel and Hobert, 2017) HPL-1 (M=0.076) or HPL-2 (M=0.083) (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 4A and B and represents colocalization analysis data.

claim: Groucho had recently been shown to compartmentalize in the nuclei of cells in Ciona.
source: We next tested if NHR-67 colocalizes with the transcriptional co-repressor Groucho, as Groucho had recently been shown to compartmentalize in the nuclei of cells in Ciona (Treen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Significant colocalization of NHR-67 punctae with LSY-22 was observed (M=0.686).
source: We observed significant colocalization of NHR-67 punctae with both LSY-22 (M=0.686) and UNC-37 (M=0.741), comparable to colocalization measures in heterozygous NHR-67::mScarlet-I/NHR-67::GFP animals (M=0.651), which were used as positive controls (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 4A and B and represents colocalization analysis data.

claim: Significant colocalization of NHR-67 punctae with UNC-37 was observed (M=0.741).
source: We observed significant colocalization of NHR-67 punctae with both LSY-22 (M=0.686) and UNC-37 (M=0.741), comparable to colocalization measures in heterozygous NHR-67::mScarlet-I/NHR-67::GFP animals (M=0.651), which were used as positive controls (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 4A and B and represents colocalization analysis data.

claim: Following AID-depletion of LSY-22, ectopic expression of an AC marker was observed in 28% of animals.
source: Following auxin treatment, we observed ectopic expression of an AC marker (cdh-3p::mCherry::moeABD) in 28% of LSY-22::AID animals and 59% of UNC-37::AID animals (n=64 for both) (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 4D and E and represents experimental data.

claim: Following AID-depletion of UNC-37, ectopic expression of an AC marker was observed in 59% of animals.
source: Following auxin treatment, we observed ectopic expression of an AC marker (cdh-3p::mCherry::moeABD) in 28% of LSY-22::AID animals and 59% of UNC-37::AID animals (n=64 for both) (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 4D and E and represents experimental data.

claim: POP-1 forms a repressive complex with UNC-37 in the early embryo to restrict expression of the endoderm-determining gene, END-1.
source: It had previously been reported that the sole TCF/LEF homolog in C. elegans, POP-1, forms a repressive complex with UNC-37 in the early embryo to restrict expression of the endoderm-determining gene, END-1 (Calvo et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: POP-1 has a known role in the development of the somatic gonad, as perturbing its function results in ectopic ACs.
source: Additionally, POP-1 has a known role in the development of the somatic gonad, as perturbing its function results in ectopic ACs (Siegfried and Kimble, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: POP-1 shows significant enrichment in the VU cells (>25%) compared to the AC.
source: Examination of an eGFP-tagged pop-1 allele (van der Horst et al., 2019), showed significant enrichment in the VU cells (>25%) compared to the AC (Figure 5B and C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to figures and represents experimental data.

claim: Endogenous POP-1 forms punctae in the nuclei of VU cells.
source: We also observed that endogenous POP-1 forms punctae in the nuclei of VU cells, which had previously been observed during interphase in non-Wnt signaled embryonic cells (Maduro et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: POP-1 punctae colocalize with NHR-67 (M=0.547).
source: These POP-1 punctae colocalize with NHR-67 (M=0.547), although to a lesser degree than UNC-37 and LSY-22, likely because the strong POP-1 fluorescence outside of punctae made them more difficult to segment (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 5D and E and represents colocalization analysis data.

claim: NHR-67(RNAi) treatment resulted in a significant increase in AC expression of eGFP::POP-1 compared to empty vector controls (225%).
source: Additionally, NHR-67(RNAi) treatment resulted in a significant increase in AC expression of eGFP::POP-1 compared to empty vector controls (225%, n>30), a pattern we observed following depletion of other transcription factors (Medwig-Kinney et al., 2020) and chromatin modifiers (Smith et al., 2022) required for AC arrest and invasion (Figure 5F and G; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to figures and represents experimental data.

claim: There is no evidence of transcriptional activation by POP-1 in the AC/VU precursors nor their differentiated descendants using an established POPTOP reporter.
source: In contrast, we did not find evidence of transcriptional activation by POP-1 in the AC/VU precursors nor their differentiated descendants using an established POPTOP (POP-1 and TCF optimal promoter) reporter, which contains seven copies of POP-1/TCF binding sites and the pes-10 minimal promoter (Figure 5H; Figure 5—figure supplement 3A and B; Green et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to figures and represents experimental data.

claim: SYS-1 (β-catenin) expression is restricted to the distal gonad early in somatic gonad development and is not detectable in the AC or VU cells.
source: Our proposed model of POP-1 acting as a repressor in the proximal gonad is consistent with the finding that SYS-1 (β-catenin) expression is restricted to the distal gonad early in somatic gonad development and is not detectable in the AC or VU cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C; Phillips et al., 2007; Sallee et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to a figure supplement and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Loss of either POP-1 and SYS-1 results in a Sys (symmetrical sister cell) phenotype, where all somatic gonad cells adopt the default proximal fate and thereby give rise to ectopic ACs.
source: Loss of either POP-1 and SYS-1 results in a Sys (symmetrical sister cell) phenotype, where all somatic gonad cells adopt the default proximal fate and thereby give rise to ectopic ACs (Siegfried and Kimble, 2002; Siegfried et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The anti-GFP nanobody was not detectable prior to or even shortly after the AC/VU cell fate decision.
source: This anti-GFP nanobody, visualized by nuclear expression of mCherry, was not detectable prior to or even shortly after the AC/VU cell fate decision, which allowed us to bypass disruption of initial cell specification (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to a figure supplement and represents experimental data.

claim: The anti-GFP nanobody produced a mild knockdown of POP-1 in the VU cells and resulted in the ectopic AC phenotype at low penetrance (7%).
source: While this method only produced a mild knockdown of POP-1 in the VU cells, we still observed the ectopic AC phenotype at low penetrance (7%, n=60) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to a figure supplement and represents experimental data.

claim: Following treatment with pop-1(RNAi), several animals with two or more bright cdh-3/lag-2+ ACs were observed (17%).
source: Following treatment with pop-1(RNAi), we observed several animals with two or more bright cdh-3/lag-2+ ACs, consistent with known phenotypes caused by cell fate misspecification in the somatic gonad (17%, n=30) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 6A and represents experimental data.

claim: Following treatment with pop-1(RNAi), animals with invasive cells that express AC markers at different levels were observed (53%).
source: We also observed animals with invasive cells that express AC markers at different levels (53%, n=30), suggesting that the cells did not adopt AC fate at the same time (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 6A and represents experimental data with an inference.

claim: Following treatment with pop-1(RNAi), a subset of ectopic ACs co-express AC markers and LAG-1, likely indicating an intermediate state between the two cell types.
source: Following treatment with pop-1(RNAi), we found that a subset of ectopic ACs co-express AC markers and LAG-1, likely indicating an intermediate state between the two cell types (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to a figure supplement and represents experimental data with an inference.

claim: Time-lapse microscopy captured ectopic ACs gradually upregulating LAG-2 (+51%) and downregulating LAG-1 (–16%) over time.
source: To visualize this process live, we used time-lapse microscopy and were able to capture ectopic ACs gradually upregulating LAG-2 (+51%, n=3) and downregulating LAG-1 (–16%, n=3) over time (Figure 6B and C), consistent with VU-to-AC cell fate conversion.
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 6B and C and represents time-lapse imaging data.

claim: Protein-protein interactions among POP-1, UNC-37, and LSY-22 have been previously identified or predicted.
source: Previous work has either directly identified or predicted protein-protein interactions among POP-1, UNC-37, and LSY-22 (Boxem et al., 2008; Calvo et al., 2001; Flowers et al., 2010; Reece-Hoyes et al., 2005; Simonis et al., 2009; Zhong and Sternberg, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: UNC-37 directly interacts with both POP-1 and LSY-22.
source: Using a yeast two-hybrid assay with UNC-37 Gal4-AD prey, we confirmed that UNC-37 directly interacts with both POP-1 and LSY-22 after observing yeast growth on the selective SC-HIS-TRP-LEU plates containing 3-AT (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to a figure supplement and represents yeast two-hybrid experimental data.

claim: NHR-67 binds directly to UNC-37.
source: Using the same technique, we found that NHR-67 binds directly to UNC-37, as previously predicted (Li et al., 2004; Simonis et al., 2009), but found no evidence of it directly interacting with LSY-22 or POP-1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to a figure supplement and represents yeast two-hybrid experimental data.

claim: There is no evidence of NHR-67 directly interacting with LSY-22 or POP-1.
source: Using the same technique, we found that NHR-67 binds directly to UNC-37, as previously predicted (Li et al., 2004; Simonis et al., 2009), but found no evidence of it directly interacting with LSY-22 or POP-1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to a figure supplement and represents yeast two-hybrid experimental data.

claim: AlphaFold and PONDR both identify an intrinsically disordered region (IDR) at the C-terminus of NHR-67.
source: To further characterize the protein-protein interaction between NHR-67 and UNC-37, we assessed the protein structure of NHR-67 using AlphaFold, an artificial intelligence-based protein structure prediction tool (Jumper et al., 2021; Varadi et al., 2022), and PONDR, a predictor of intrinsic disorder (Peng and Zhang, 2006). Both identify an intrinsically disordered region (IDR) at the C-terminus of NHR-67 (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 7A and B and represents computational prediction data.

claim: The 108 amino acid IDR sequence of NHR-67 is necessary and sufficient to bind with UNC-37.
source: Yeast growth on the selective SC-HIS-TRP-LEU plates containing the competitive inhibitor 3-aminotriazole (3-AT) demonstrates that the 108 amino acid IDR sequence of NHR-67 is necessary and sufficient to bind with UNC-37 (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 7C and D and represents yeast two-hybrid experimental data.

claim: UNC-37, LSY-22, and POP-1 contribute to the repression of the default invasive state in VU cells.
source: Through functional perturbations, we demonstrate that UNC-37, LSY-22, and POP-1 contribute to the repression of the default invasive state in VU cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 4, 5, and 6.

claim: NHR-67 punctae exhibit liquid-like properties similar to what has been described with P granules.
source: We also discovered that NHR-67 forms nuclear foci in non-invasive cells, which exhibit liquid-like properties, indicated by observations of their condensation, dissolution, and relatively rapid recovery from photobleaching, similar to what has been described with P granules (Brangwynne et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by experimental data in Figure 3 and a citation to published literature.

claim: The association of NHR-67 with Groucho leads to protein condensation, as has recently been described in Ciona embryos.
source: We postulate that this association leads to protein condensation, as has recently been described in Ciona embryos (Treen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a postulation stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The dynamic punctae formed by POP-1 in non-Wnt signaled cells was first described 20 years ago.
source: It is also interesting to note that the dynamic punctae formed by POP-1 in non-Wnt signaled cells was first described 20 years ago (Maduro et al., 2002), but their function is only now being appreciated in light of recent advances in our understanding of the formation of higher-order associations in the nucleus.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: This is the second observed case of compartmentalization of Groucho proteins.
source: Here, we report the second observed case of compartmentalization of Groucho proteins (Treen et al., 2021), which may suggest that Groucho proteins have evolutionarily conserved roles that require this type of subnuclear organization.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Groucho proteins may have evolutionarily conserved roles that require subnuclear organization.
source: Here, we report the second observed case of compartmentalization of Groucho proteins (Treen et al., 2021), which may suggest that Groucho proteins have evolutionarily conserved roles that require this type of subnuclear organization.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion based on inference from the data.

claim: It is unknown whether DNA binding is necessary for nuclear puncta formation.
source: For example, it is unknown whether DNA binding is necessary for nuclear puncta formation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an open question.

claim: The interaction between UNC-37 and NHR-67 does not appear to depend on DNA binding.
source: The interaction between UNC-37 and NHR-67 does not appear to depend on DNA binding, as the C-terminal IDR region of NHR-67 (excluding its zinc finger domains) was sufficient for binding with UNC-37 in vitro, but it is possible that DNA binding is needed for oligomerization in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by yeast two-hybrid data in Figure 7.

claim: It is possible that DNA binding is needed for oligomerization in vivo.
source: The interaction between UNC-37 and NHR-67 does not appear to depend on DNA binding, as the C-terminal IDR region of NHR-67 (excluding its zinc finger domains) was sufficient for binding with UNC-37 in vitro, but it is possible that DNA binding is needed for oligomerization in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion.

claim: It remains unclear if suppression of invasive differentiation is achieved by simply sequestering NHR-67 away from its transcriptional targets or through direct repression of transcription.
source: Furthermore, it remains unclear if suppression of invasive differentiation is achieved by simply sequestering the pro-invasive transcription factor NHR-67 away from its transcriptional targets or through direct repression of transcription.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an open question.

claim: Direct targets of NHR-67 have not yet been discovered.
source: Direct targets of NHR-67 have not yet been discovered, which makes it difficult to investigate this specific aspect of the repressive mechanism at present.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a limitation of the current study.

claim: G1 arrest has been shown to enhance the conversion of human fibroblasts to dopaminergic neurons.
source: While G1 arrest has been shown to enhance the conversion of human fibroblasts to dopaminergic neurons (Jiang et al., 2015), mitosis is required for the natural K-to-DVB transdifferentiation event in C. elegans (Riva et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Mitosis is required for the natural K-to-DVB transdifferentiation event in C. elegans.
source: While G1 arrest has been shown to enhance the conversion of human fibroblasts to dopaminergic neurons (Jiang et al., 2015), mitosis is required for the natural K-to-DVB transdifferentiation event in C. elegans (Riva et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to published literature.
